name: Refugees International (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: shares of the result by branch at the defaults. Haitians paroled into the US (about 42%, counted as Haiti's), Sudan's humanitarian response and access from Chad (about 23%), asylum seekers' work permits in Costa Rica (about 5%); the other campaigns (about 30%) over Ukraine, Gaza, the US and Uganda by the annual report's emphasis (a judgment).
summary: Refugees International, a Washington advocacy group that takes no government money, spent $4.5m on advocacy and strategic outreach in 2024 (its latest full audited year). No outcome is measured, so each of its main 2024 results is built from public data and ranged judgments and counted at half by the shared missing-data slider: the roughly 97,000 Haitians paroled into the US that year under pathways it pressed for, valued by their gain in consumption and health, and their remittances home, for the years they stay; Sudan's $1.9bn 2024 humanitarian response, of which advocacy is credited with a small share, net of the aid it displaced, and the aid the reopened Adre crossing let through; and Costa Rica's June 2024 reform giving asylum seekers work permits, from a study of regularisation in Colombia; other campaigns add 42%. It comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per $1,000 (plausible range {{range}}): about two fifths from Haiti, a quarter from Sudan, a twentieth from Costa Rica and the rest from the other campaigns. The result is mostly uncertainty: the biggest questions are how much of each result advocacy caused, Refugees International's share of the advocacy, and how long the parolees stay.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Value of a dollar moved (shared)
sections.explainer: charityevals' shared method for money a meta charity moves, the same rows in every such model (docs/normalization.md 2.8). A dollar moved is worth what the charities it reaches achieve, each at its live result on this site under your values; new money counts in full, shifted money only for the gain over where it would have gone.

sections.title: Career changes
sections.explainer: People the charity moves into high-impact jobs: per career changed, the pay they give up for the years they stay, valued at the new employer's live result per dollar, times the share of changes the charity caused (docs/normalization.md 2.8). The mirror of staff pay below market.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Haiti: Haitians paroled into the US in 2024
rows.explainer: The nine months' arrivals scaled to a year: about 97,000, close to Refugees International's own 'over 100,000 Haitians' for 2024 (financial statements, note 1, p. 8). The processes were briefly paused in July-August 2024 for vetting checks, which the scaling averages in. These are the people Refugees International's advocacy for the Haitian parole pathway is credited with helping, below. Its accounts also claim the expansion of family-reunification parole for Haitians and Cubans; those arrivals (a few thousand a year, not published by year in a source we could read) are in the other campaigns' share (below).

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption per person in the US (US$ a year)
rows.explainer: The Consumer Expenditure Survey's spending per person (the site's US baseline, docs/normalization.md 2.14) times the shared share for refugees and migrants who reach a rich country (@irap.destination_consumption_share, 0.45, from 0.3 to 0.7, anchored on the lowest-income fifth's spending): about $14,700. Parolees had work authorisation and a US sponsor, mostly in low-wage jobs.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption at home relative to the average Haitian
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-3): the process needed a passport, a flight and a US sponsor with means, so parolees came from better-off households than the average Haitian; 1 if they were typical, 3 if mostly urban middle class.

rows.label: Haiti: parolees' consumption per person had they stayed (US$ a year at US prices)
rows.explainer: Haiti's national-accounts consumption per person (2024) on the survey scale (the site's median survey-to-national-accounts ratio: Haiti has no recent survey), at US prices of the same year (the 2024 private-consumption PPP factor), times the judgment above: about $2,500.

rows.label: Haiti: gain in log consumption per person-year in the US
rows.explainer: ln(consumption in the US ÷ consumption at home), on the site's one log-income scale, as cash-income does.

rows.label: Haiti: years the adult mortality rate spans (ages 15 to 60)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: mortality rate, adult (SP.DYN.AMRT.MA), definition
source.quote: Adult mortality rate is the probability of dying between the ages of 15 and 60

rows.explainer: The definition of the adult mortality rate: the chance of dying between exact ages 15 and 60.

rows.label: Haiti: share of the adult death-rate gap between Haiti and the US that a parolee escapes
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-90%): in the US parolees face US rates of violence, infection and maternal death, but newly arrived low-income migrants have less health care than the average American (and some arrive with untreated conditions). It covers the gang violence of 2023-2024 (at least 5,601 killed in 2024, UN News) and Haiti's weak health system alike.

rows.label: Haiti: deaths averted per person-year in the US
rows.formula: (ln(1 - avg(hai_adult_mortality_usa_male, hai_adult_mortality_usa_female)) - ln(1 - avg(hai_adult_mortality_hti_male, hai_adult_mortality_hti_female))) / hai_adult_mortality_span * hai_mortality_gap_removed
rows.explainer: The yearly adult death rate in Haiti less the US's (each from the chance of dying between 15 and 60, men and women averaged: -ln(1 - q) over 45 years; about 0.0029 a year), times the share escaped.

rows.label: Haiti: share of parolees who wouldn't otherwise have reached the US
rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-90%): without the lawful pathway some would have crossed irregularly (Haitians were among the largest groups at the southern border in 2021-2022) and some would have gone to other countries (Chile, Brazil, the Dominican Republic) with smaller gains; most had no other way to leave.

rows.label: Haiti: share of the parolees' deaths averted that are of children
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (10-35%): families came with their children under the processes, but the adult death-rate gap is the one counted and children's death rates are lower; their deaths are valued at the 5-14 band.

rows.label: Haiti: share of adults' deaths averted that are under 50
rows.explainer: Judgment 60% (40-80%): the gap counted is of ages 15 to 60, where death rates rise with age, so much of it falls at 50-59 (valued at the 50-74 band); most parolees are young adults.

rows.label: Haiti: value of a death averted among parolees (units of value)
rows.explainer: The shared moral weights by age band, mixed by the shares above, times the value-of-life slider.

rows.label: Haiti: parolee's own gain per year in the US (units of value)
rows.explainer: The log-consumption gain plus the deaths averted, for the share who wouldn't otherwise have come.

rows.label: Haiti: value per parolee per year in the US (units of value)
rows.explainer: The parolee's own gain plus the remittances home (a side effect), for the share who wouldn't otherwise have come.

rows.label: Haiti: years a parolee stays in the US
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 (1.5-15): parole was for two years, and the processes were ended in 2025 (DHS terminated CHNV in March 2025); many applied for asylum or Temporary Protected Status, or stayed without status, and few were removed to Haiti while its airports and capital were under gang control. 1.5 if most leave or are removed when parole ends, 15 if most settle.

rows.label: Haiti: years in the US, discounted
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate. A parolee's years are their own, not a won reform's (rights-advocacy: a released person's years), so not $win_years_counted.

rows.label: Haiti: money a parolee sends home a year (US$)

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: personal remittances, received (BX.TRF.PWKR.CD.DT), 2024
source.note: https://api.worldbank.org/v2/country/HTI/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.CD.DT?format=json&date=2024; the anchor, not the row's value

rows.explainer: Judgment $1,500 ($500-$3,000): Haiti received $4.1bn of personal remittances in 2024 (World Bank), mostly from the US, home to most of its 1.5-2 million emigrants: about $2,000-2,700 per emigrant. Less for new arrivals in their first low-wage years, more for those sending to children left behind.

rows.label: Haiti: people at home sharing what a parolee sends
rows.explainer: Judgment 4 (2-6): a household in Haiti (about four people) or parents and siblings.

rows.label: Haiti: value of remittances to family at home, per parolee-year (units of value)
rows.explainer: A side effect: the recipients' gain on the log scale, n × ln(1 + sent / (n × their consumption)), their consumption that of the parolee's household at home (above). The parolee's own US consumption above is spending, already net of what is sent.

rows.label: Haiti: loss to Haiti from the departure of skilled people, as a share of the parolees' own gain
rows.explainer: A side effect: nurses, teachers and other skilled workers were among those who left. Judgment -7% (-20% to -2%) of the parolees' own gain: the parolees are a small share of Haiti's workforce (about 1%); gross of remittances, which are their own row.

rows.label: Haiti: value of 2024's parolees (units of value)
rows.explainer: Parolees × discounted years × (value per person-year less the loss to Haiti, a side effect on the parolees' own gain). A year's arrivals against a year's spending (the pathways had to be defended each year: a Texas-led lawsuit against them was dismissed in March 2024).

rows.label: Sudan: humanitarian funding to the 2024 response plan (US$)

source.title: OCHA Financial Tracking Service, Sudan Humanitarian Response Plan 2024 (plan 1188)
source.note: Read from the FTS public API, https://api.hpc.tools/v1/public/fts/flow?planId=1188&groupby=plan

rows.explainer: Funding reported to OCHA's Financial Tracking Service against Sudan's 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan ($2.70bn required, about 70% funded; 2023's plan was 51% funded, $1.32bn of $2.57bn, FTS plan 1123). Refugees International's 'Speak Out on Sudan' campaign with diaspora groups pressed for aid, access and diplomacy throughout 2024.

rows.label: Sudan: value of a dollar of Sudan's 2024 response relative to the average humanitarian response
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-2.5): famine was confirmed in Zamzam camp in August 2024 (the Famine Review Committee) and death rates were far above the emergency threshold, so food, water, health care and cash reaching people avert more deaths per dollar than the average response; access problems and diversion by the warring parties pull it back.

rows.label: Sudan: value of a dollar of the response, as a multiple of cash
rows.explainer: The site's shared value of a dollar of humanitarian aid (@aid_value.humanitarian_vs_cash, 0.2× cash: the site's relief models before their missing-data step; docs/normalization.md 2.20) times Sudan's famine premium above.

rows.label: Sudan: value of a dollar of the response (units of value)
rows.explainer: The multiple × the site's value of a dollar given as cash (@cash.uov_per_dollar).

rows.label: Sudan: share of the extra funding taken from other aid
rows.explainer: Judgment 50% (20-80%): donors' humanitarian budgets are mostly set, so money that advocacy steers to Sudan partly comes from other crises; some is new (supplementary appropriations, pledging conferences such as Paris in April 2024).

rows.label: Sudan: value of the other aid displaced, per dollar (units of value)
rows.explainer: A side effect: the displaced aid's value, lost, at the shared value of a dollar of humanitarian aid (@aid_value.humanitarian_vs_cash: the other crises it is taken from).

rows.label: Sudan: years until the funding is spent
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.5 (0.25-1): funding to a response plan is spent within the year or soon after.

rows.label: Sudan: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Sudan: value of the 2024 response funding (units of value)
rows.explainer: Funding × (the value of a dollar less the aid it displaces), discounted for the wait. A year's funding against a year's spending; the share advocacy added and Refugees International's part are below.

rows.label: Sudan access: share of 2024's response that reached people only through the access the campaign pressed for
rows.explainer: Judgment 2% (0.5-8%): the campaign pressed for the Adre crossing from Chad (reopened on 15 August 2024 after six months closed), the main route into Darfur, and for access across the lines; a part of the year's aid went through it after August, and some would have gone through Tine or across lines anyway.

rows.label: Sudan access: value of the aid let through (units of value)
rows.explainer: The year's funding × the share let through by the access gains × the value of a dollar of Sudan's response, discounted like the funding. No aid is displaced: access lets the same money reach more people. The envoy, the genocide determination and pressure on the UAE are in the other campaigns' share.

rows.label: Costa Rica: work permits issued a year to asylum seekers under the 2024 rules

source.title: UNHCR, Costa Rica Annual Results Report 2024
source.quote: enabling the issuance of 20,000 work permits and the renewal of 22,000
source.note: UNHCR's site returns 403 to automated fetches; the sentence as shown in search results on 2026-11-14. The decree's content (automatic work authorisation from July 2024) is confirmed by Refugees International's April 2026 Costa Rica report, https://d3jwam0i5codb7.cloudfront.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CRReportENGApril2026_FINAL.pdf.

rows.explainer: UNHCR credits Executive Decree 44501-MGP (12 June 2024), which partly reversed the 2022 decree 43810-MGP that had removed asylum seekers' immediate work permits, with 20,000 work permits issued (and 22,000 renewed) in 2024. Taken as a year's flow: the first months cleared a backlog, and about 2,100 new asylum claims arrive each month (UNHCR, 2024), about 25,000 a year who need permits. The publisher blocks automated downloads; figure from its 2024 Annual Results Report as indexed.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share of those permits that the 2022 rules would have blocked

source.title: Refugees International, Strengthening the Integration of Asylum Seekers and Refugees in Costa Rica (April 2026)
source.quote: This reform eliminated the requirement to present proof of employment or submit a separate work permit application
source.note: UNHCR, Costa Rica factsheet January-June 2024, https://www.unhcr.org/sites/default/files/2024-09/240902%20Costa%20Rica%20Factsheet%20jan-jun2024_ENG_VF.pdf (403 to automated fetches; its 222 requested and 55 approved permits in 2023 as summarised by search, unconfirmed).

rows.explainer: Judgment 70% (40-90%): Refugees International's April 2026 report says the July 2024 reform removed the need for proof of employment and a separate permit application, and covered self-employment; under the 2022 decree a permit needed a job and social-security enrolment after a three-month wait, and UNHCR's January-June 2024 factsheet (as indexed in search results; unhcr.org blocks automated reading) reports only 55 of 222 requests approved in 2023. Not all: some would have got a permit later, or worked informally anyway.

rows.label: Costa Rica: people sharing the gain of one permit
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-2.5): the gain is in household consumption per person, shared with children and partners; many households have more than one permit holder.

rows.label: Costa Rica: people a year gaining from the right to work
rows.explainer: Permits a year × the share the reform made possible × the people sharing each.

rows.label: Costa Rica: consumption gain from regularisation for forced migrants (Colombia's PEP)

source.title: Ibáñez, Moya, Ortega, Rozo and Urbina, Life out of the Shadows: Impacts of Amnesties in the Lives of Refugees (IZA DP 15049, 2022; JEEA 2025)
source.quote: consumption per capita (a gain of 48%), monthly labor income (an increase of 22%)
source.note: The published abstract (Journal of the European Economic Association 23(3), 2025, pp. 941-982); the 2022 working paper (https://docs.iza.org/dp15049.pdf) reports 60 percent.

rows.explainer: Ibáñez et al. (Life out of the Shadows, IZA DP 15049; Journal of the European Economic Association 2025), a natural experiment on Venezuelan migrants in Colombia: regularisation under the PEP raised consumption per person by 60% in the working paper and 48% in the published version. Best guess the published figure; range from 30% to the working paper's 60%.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share of the regularisation effect that a work permit alone brings
rows.explainer: Judgment 40% (15-70%): the PEP gave legal status, work rights, health insurance and bank accounts; asylum seekers in Costa Rica already had legal stay, and the 2024 change adds a work permit from the start and self-employment. The paper attributes much of the gain to access to services, not only work.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value per person per year (units of value)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + the consumption gain a work permit brings) × the site's value of a doubling of consumption.

rows.label: Costa Rica: chance the change happens
rows.explainer: The decree was issued in June 2024 and applied from July, so 1; how much was advocates' doing is the counterfactual below.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years the change counts
rows.explainer: A won reform counts the site's shared years brought forward ($win_years_counted, docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Costa Rica: years until the change takes effect
rows.explainer: Judgment 0.1 (0-0.3): published in June 2024, permits on the new cards from July.

rows.label: Costa Rica: discount for the wait
rows.explainer: At the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years counted, discounted
rows.explainer: The years counted, discounted, after the wait.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value of the reform (units of value)
rows.explainer: People a year × value per person-year × the chance × the discounted years counted.

rows.label: Costa Rica: years of campaigning behind the win
rows.explainer: Judgment 1.5 (1-2.5): Refugees International and IRCA Casabierta, a refugee-led organisation, contested the November 2022 decrees from their issue (joint statement, December 2022) until the June 2024 reform.

rows.label: Costa Rica: value per year of campaigning, at 2024's budget (units of value)
rows.explainer: The win over the years of spending behind it, scaled to 2024's budget, so it sets against the 2024 cost.

rows.label: Other campaigns' results, as a share of the three modelled campaigns
rows.explainer: Judgment 42% (11-150%): the 2024 annual report names other work with no measured result: localisation of aid in Ukraine (two reports it says led to more aid from state donors directly to Ukrainian organisations), the Gaza scorecard with seven other agencies on aid obstruction, LGBTQ+ refugees' access to jobs in Costa Rica, the Destination Reception Assistance Act it helped draft and the #LetAsylumSeekersWork bill (neither passed), climate displacement at COP29 and in Uganda's adaptation plan, the Refugee Fellows, the Refugee Advocacy Lab's public support for US resettlement (about 500 state and local officials' letter), and family-reunification parole for Haitians and Cubans (a few thousand arrivals a year, against the 97,000 counted above). The US envoy, the genocide determination and pressure on the UAE over Sudan are here too. Anchor: the eight other campaigns against the three modelled, each worth 15% of an average modelled win, plus family reunification at 5%: (8 × 15% + 5%) / 3 = 42%; 11% at 4% each and 1% (they mostly changed words), 150% at 55% each and 10% (Ukraine's localisation moved large sums).

rows.label: Haiti parole: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.5-1): the gain is a cross-country consumption gap, not measured for these parolees; studies of migrants' earnings at the same skill (the 'place premium') find gains as large or larger, but parolees' first years are below their later earnings.

rows.label: Haiti parole: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 10% (3-30%): the processes were the administration's own border policy, launched in January 2023 alongside expulsions at the border; advocates pressed for Haitians' inclusion, family reunification and keeping the pathway open. 3% if it would have run the same without them, 30% if advocacy kept it going against the 2024 lawsuit and political pressure.

rows.label: Haiti parole: Refugees International's share of the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 5% (2-15%): many groups pressed for the Haitian pathways (Haitian Bridge Alliance, Welcome.US, the resettlement agencies, IRAP, HIAS, the Haitian diaspora, members of Congress); Refugees International names its part in its 2024 accounts, as one of several Washington voices.

rows.label: Haiti parole: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Haiti parole: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: the arrivals are counted, but the advocacy's part and the parolees' gains are judgments, not measured. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Haiti parole: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Sudan: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 1: the dollar's value is the shared figure, already net of the relief models' own evidence adjustments; Sudan's difference from the average is sdn_response_vs_average, and the lack of measurement is the missing-data step (one question per adjustment, Convention 5).

rows.label: Sudan: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 3% (1-8%) of 2024's Sudan funding added by advocacy as a whole: funding rose from 51% of the plan in 2023 (FTS, plan 1123) to 70% in 2024, mostly from the famine and the scale of the war; advocates moved the margin. 1% if donors would have given the same, 8% if the campaign held up the US's and other large donors' pledges.

rows.label: Sudan: Refugees International's share of the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 4.5% (2-12%): Refugees International's leverage is in Washington, and the US gave 45% of the 2024 plan's funding (FTS, plan 1188 by donor: the US government $738.9m and the State Department $106.6m of $1,889m); of US advocacy on Sudan it had about a tenth, one of about ten groups: 45% × 10% = 4.5%. It was one of the main US voices on Sudan in 2024 (its President testified and led the 'Speak Out on Sudan' campaign with diaspora groups), beside the IRC, NRC, MSF, Oxfam, Save the Children, Mercy Corps, Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and the UN agencies themselves.

rows.label: Sudan: share of credit used
rows.explainer: The share among co-advocates times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: Sudan: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: Thin: no measured effect of the campaign on funding or access. Counted less by the shared slider (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Sudan: all adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Costa Rica: evidence adjustment
rows.explainer: 0.8 (0.5-1): external validity only (the narrower change is cri_work_permit_share_of_effect): Venezuelans in Colombia, not Nicaraguans in Costa Rica, and the published paper's 48% against the working paper's 60%.

rows.label: Costa Rica: share that wouldn't have happened without the advocacy
rows.explainer: Judgment 20% (5-50%): the share of the reform due to advocates at all. The Constitutional Court had already struck down another part of the 2022 decree, UNHCR pressed the government, and the backlog made the old rules costly to run; advocates' pressure moved the timing and content.

rows.label: Costa Rica: Refugees International's share of the advocacy

rows.label: Value of a dollar where shifted money would otherwise have gone (our judgment: 1× GiveDirectly), units of value
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Shifted money was going to be given anyway; it is credited only for the gain. Where it would have gone is valued at GiveDirectly's live result (GiveWell's model), as Ambitious Impact does, times a shared multiple (1×, from 0 to 3×).

rows.explainer: The site's one figure for every meta charity: about half the money moved wouldn't otherwise have been given (Ambitious Impact's Effective Giving Incubation report), from 35% to 80%.

rows.label: Value of a dollar moved, net of where shifted money would have gone, at the mobiliser's share, units of value
rows.explainer: New money counts in full; shifted money counts for the gain over where it would have gone. The donors gave it, so the organisation is credited its share of that good (mobiliser_share).
